audits.mathematicalReason: Using the tangencies shown, the rectangle's width equals the circle's diameter, 2×5=10. The 2:1 length-to-width ratio gives length 20, so the area is 20×10=200. Rectangle area is an appropriate assessed scope, supported by the radius–diameter relationship and the meaning of the side ratio.
limitations: The answer uses tangency to the two long sides shown in the figure. Under the strict meaning of an inscribed circle tangent to all four sides, the rectangle would have to be a square, contradicting the 2:1 ratio. The candidate appropriately acknowledges this wording issue.

figureEvidence.fact: The circle touches the upper and lower horizontal sides of the rectangle, while leaving gaps to both vertical sides; thus the depicted short dimension is one diameter.

audits.mathematicalReason: Tangency gives CB perpendicular to AD. Since C is also the outer circle's center, this perpendicular bisects the chord, so AB=8. Writing r=CB, Pythagoras gives r²=10²−8²=36. The annular area is π(100−36)=64π. Alternatively, apply inner-circle tangent–secant power from A along the line through C: 8²=(10−r)(10+r)=100−r². Both listed routes are valid alternatives. Combining disk areas by subtraction supports the composite-area assessment and circle-area support.

figureEvidence.fact: A and D lie on the outer circle, C is the common center, and B lies on both chord AD and the inner circle. The right-angle marker shows CB perpendicular to AD at B.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the inner length be L>0. The nested rectangles have dimensions L×1, (L+2)×3, and (L+4)×5. Their three colored region areas are L, 3(L+2)−L=2L+6, and 5(L+4)−3(L+2)=2L+14. These are increasing for L>0. The arithmetic-progression condition gives 2(2L+6)=L+(2L+14), hence L=2. The areas are then 2, 10, and 18 square feet. The assessed arithmetic-mean relation and composite-area subtraction, with rectangle-area and simple-equation support, are appropriate.

figureEvidence.fact: The three colors occupy the inner rectangle and two surrounding rectangular borders. The inner width is labeled 1, and the border offsets are labeled 1; together with the stated uniform widths, each added border increases both dimensions by 2 feet.

audits.mathematicalReason: The whole field has area 10×8=80 square meters. Removing the one-meter reachable strip from both ends of each dimension leaves an unreachable rectangle measuring 8×6, with area 48. The reachable area is therefore 80−48=32 square meters, and its fraction of the whole is 32/80=2/5. Composite-area subtraction and the part-to-whole meaning of a fraction are appropriate assessed scopes; rectangle area and reduction are appropriate support.

figureEvidence.fact: The outer rectangle is labeled 10 m by 8 m. The shaded region surrounds all four sides of an inset unshaded rectangle, and the border thickness is labeled 1 m.

audits.mathematicalReason: Adjacent shaded vertices have horizontal and vertical separations 3 and 1 units. Thus the shaded square's side length squared, and therefore its area, is 3²+1²=10. Alternatively, the axis-aligned bounding square has side 4, and its four corner triangles each have legs 3 and 1. Subtraction gives 4²−4(3×1/2)=10. The square-area assessment and both alternative routes are defensible; neither route must be required universally.

figureEvidence.fact: Counting the unit grid, the top shaded vertex is three units right and one row above the left shaded vertex. The right vertex is one unit right and three rows below the top vertex. These positions also give a 4-by-4 axis-aligned bounding square.

audits.mathematicalReason: The graph starts at 0 miles and 0 hours and ends at 35 miles and 7 hours. Average speed for the entire ride is total distance divided by total elapsed time: 35/7=5 miles per hour. The intermediate segment speeds do not need to be averaged. Reading the line graph and applying the distance–speed–time relationship match the candidate scopes.

figureEvidence.fact: The horizontal axis is Hours and the vertical axis is Miles. The plotted ride begins at (0,0) and ends at (7,35).

audits.mathematicalReason: Clockwise rolling to the right places the sides on consecutive intervals in the order AB, BC, CD, DE, EA. Their total length is 3+4+6+3+7=23, after which the contact pattern repeats. Since 2009=87×23+8, examine position 8 in one cycle. AB covers 0 to 3, BC covers 3 to 7, and CD covers 7 to 13, so position 8 lies strictly inside CD's interval. Remainder reasoning is appropriate, with segment addition as support; there is no vertex-boundary ambiguity.

audits.mathematicalReason: A unit regular hexagon has circumradius 1 and apothem √3/2, as follows from its equilateral subdivisions and Pythagoras. Place the central hexagon's center at (0,0), with its left and right vertices at (−1,0) and (1,0). The pictured tiling then gives A=(−2,0), B=(1,√3), and C=(1,−√3). Consequently BC=2√3, and the perpendicular distance from A to BC is 3. The triangle's area is (1/2)(2√3)(3)=3√3. The candidate's regular-polygon and triangle-area scopes, with equilateral-triangle and Pythagorean support, describe a valid method.

figureEvidence.fact: The seven regular hexagons share complete sides. A is horizontally aligned with the central hexagon's left and right vertices, one hexagon side to the left of its left vertex. B and C are vertically aligned with the central hexagon's right vertex, at the indicated vertices of the upper-right and lower-right surrounding hexagons.
